children: Iron ore prices rose for a third straight session on Monday to hit a more than one-month high, supported by elevated freight rates and expectations of restocking by steelmakers ahead of the National Day holiday in top consumer China.
The most-traded iron ore contract on China's Dalian Commodity Exchange (DCE)
climbed 1.52% to 727 yuan ($108.33) a metric ton by 0149 GMT, after touching its highest since July 30 at 739 yuan earlier in the session.

The benchmark October iron ore (SZZFV6) on the Singapore Exchange rose 1.27% to $100.9 a ton by 0139 GMT, the highest since July 15 and trading above the key psychological level of $100 for a second straight session.
Lending support to the key steelmaking ingredient was rallying freight rates fueled by strong energy prices amid renewed tensions between the United States and Iran, said analysts.
Moreover, anticipation of growing appetite for steelmaking ingredients as steel demand seasonally picks up this month also boosted market sentiment.

Ore consumption has shown signs of recovery with average daily hot metal output, a gauge of iron ore demand, ticking up 0.1% from the week before to 2.37 million tons, as of September 4, after two weeks of falls, data from consultancy Mysteel showed.
However, thin steel margins curbed gains in ore prices, according to Guiqiu Zhuo, an analyst at broker Jinrui Futures.
"There is a seesaw effect between iron ore and coal, with the former strengthening while the latter weakening, but steel margins remained squeezed," said Zhuo.
